evidence_cards.title: MEPS 2016: people with a reported ICD-10 A69 (other spirochetal infections, which includes Lyme disease)
evidence_cards.definition: People with at least one condition record whose 3-character ICD10CDX equals A69.
evidence_cards.method: Sum of unique-person weights (PERWT16F) over the domain; standard error by Taylor linearisation over VARSTR/VARPSU. Person-level, one year only.
comparability: A69 is the broad category that contains Lyme (A69.2x); MEPS public files keep only the first 3 characters, so this is NOT a Lyme-specific count and must not be read as Lyme prevalence.
MEPS panels overlap across adjacent years: never add or pool these yearly totals.
Condition rows come from household reports coded by professional coders.

AHRQ (MEPS team, 2026-09-24) urges caution forming Lyme cost estimates from MEPS: pooling 2016-2024 gives only about 300-400 observations, expenditures are highly skewed (about 1,000 or more are needed for a solid mean), only treated Lyme is identified (zero-expenditure cases drop out, biasing upward), events may be flagged as arthritis without naming Lyme, comorbidities cannot be separated from Lyme, and onset dates are not recorded. Lyme-specific A69.2 is available only in restricted data centers.

uncertainty.note: Small samples give very wide, unreliable intervals.

evidence_cards.summary: 2016: about 436,208 people (95% CI 250,739 to 621,678; 31 sampled persons) reported a condition coded A69.
evidence_cards.how_to_use: Cross-check or population context only, never a prevalence of Lyme or Long COVID; not a cost estimate (events are counts, not dollars).

spec.title: Chronic Lyme Disease Patient-Reported Burden Simulator (Johnson et al. 2014)
spec.boundary: This simulation reproduces descriptive comparisons from a 2014 self-selected internet survey of 3,090 people with chronic Lyme disease (CLD), contrasted with published general-population figures the authors cite (NHIS, BLS/general-population employment, CDC surveillance). It does not compute a total medical-expenditure dollar figure or a dollar value of lost productivity, because the study itself states it was not designed to do either. All CLD figures come from a non-probability, forum-recruited sample and cannot be generalized to all Lyme disease patients.

takeaway.patient: In this 2014 patient survey, people with long-lasting Lyme disease symptoms were far more likely than the general population to report high annual out-of-pocket costs, to have stopped or cut back working, and to have waited years for a diagnosis. These are patterns reported by a self-selected group of patients who joined Lyme disease forums, not a guarantee of what will happen to any one person, but they may reflect experiences you recognize in your own care.
takeaway.care: This survey found markedly higher healthcare-seeking behavior, employment loss, and out-of-pocket spending among patients with persistent post-treatment Lyme symptoms compared with general-population benchmarks, alongside long typical delays before diagnosis. The findings suggest persistent-symptom Lyme patients may benefit from coordinated follow-up and realistic expectations about insurance coverage for extended treatment, though the study cannot say why utilization was higher or whether earlier diagnosis would have changed outcomes.
takeaway.policy: The study documents a large gap between chronic Lyme disease respondents and general-population benchmarks in out-of-pocket spending, employment, and diagnostic delay, alongside a separate, long-standing gap between CDC's restrictive surveillance case count and its broader case-finding estimate. ## Source
Johnson et al. (2014, PeerJ) surveyed 3,090 self-selected, forum-recruited respondents with chronic Lyme disease (CLD) - clinically diagnosed Lyme disease with symptoms persisting over six months after treatment - using CDC's 9-item health-related quality of life items, and compared results to published general-population and NHIS/BLS/CDC figures. The authors explicitly state the study was not designed to calculate total medical expenditures or a dollar value of lost productivity, so this simulator reports only percentages and case counts, never a cost total.

## Parameters
Out-of-pocket cost shares (>$5,000/year) use the Results/Table 4 full-sample figure (43.2%) versus an NHIS 2011 general-population comparator (~6%); the Discussion section separately states 46% vs 5% for the same threshold, an inconsistency the document itself does not resolve. Employment rates (25-54) and the two-year diagnostic-delay share are taken directly from the paper's reported figures. The CDC case-count inputs reflect two structurally different case-ascertainment methods: a restrictive surveillance definition (~30,000/year) versus a broader approach using self-reported diagnosis, insurance coding, and serology (~300,000/year, cited for 2013); the document does not call either number a corrected 'true' incidence, and this simulator does not either.

## Limitations
The CDC's ~300,000 estimate relies partly on insurance/claims coding and self-reported diagnosis rather than confirmed surveillance criteria; claims-based approaches like this generally understate true disease prevalence, even though here the broader estimate already exceeds the stricter surveillance figure, which the document attributes to the surveillance definition itself undercounting.

All pooled CLD figures (cost, employment, diagnostic delay) are reported only for the full sample, with no breakdown by sex, age, race/ethnicity, or income, despite these being collected. Federal survey data sources such as MEPS, NHIS, and BRFSS generally support disaggregated analysis even though this document did not perform one here.

The document separately describes a surveillance/data gap - noting little population-level data exists on Lyme disease's impact on quality of life and work capacity, and recommending CDC/NIH add Lyme-specific items to national surveys - and a distinct coverage/regulatory gap, noting many insurers restrict coverage of extended Lyme antibiotic therapy.

The CLD sample is self-selected and non-probability; it should not be statistically pooled with general-population benchmarks drawn from different sampling frames and years. No lifetime-cost or multi-year model is provided; all figures are annual, point-in-time self-reports.

## Federal cross-check (computed by the system, not by the AI model)

The model only read these quantities from the document; the comparisons below were calculated in code from federal data files. The federal figures are published or surveyed values; the simulator's own outputs are modeled from the uploaded document.

- CDC estimated annual U.S. Lyme disease diagnoses (2013, the United States): the document's estimate of 300,000 is 8.3 times the 36,307 cases CDC received as reported. Reported cases are a passive-surveillance subset, so estimates from claims or models are usually higher; this shows the size of the gap, not which figure is right. Federal source: public health surveillance (surveillance report), 2008-2021; computed in code from the federal file; no AI model.
